summary: A poem titled Remembrances of Things Past, published as an informational RFC. It is a lighthearted reflection on the early days of networking and not a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a poem, not a rulebook. A person wrote about remembering old times in the computer networks they helped build.

subtitle: A poem of puns on computing and networking words, remembering when they meant something else.

tldr.problem: Computing and networking vocabulary has changed, and words once had everyday meanings that the field has taken over.
tldr.mechanism: The memo is a rhyming poem that pairs each technical word with its older meaning, such as a router being a tool and a server being a maid.
tldr.outcome: It specifies nothing. It is an Informational poem that says it does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 1300 is an Informational document and, according to its metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It contains no protocol, so there is nothing to implement.

sections.title: A Poem in an RFC
sections.content:
RFC 1300 by Stanley R. Greenfield of Ziff-Davis, dated February 1992, is a poem under the heading "Discussion". Its status section says only that it provides information and does not specify an Internet standard.

The poem is a long run of two-line contrasts. It looks back to a time when technical words had other meanings, and it is signed "--srg".
sections.plainLanguage: This is a poem filed in a collection of technical papers. It has no rules in it, just rhymes.

sections.title: The Wordplay
sections.content:
Every couplet swaps a modern term for an older sense. A router was a tool and a server was a maid. Windows were for looking out of, bridges were for crossing, and a frame was for keeping pictures in. A buffer was for buffing, and a plotter was called a CAD.

The poem opens with "When Shannon was a river and Turing was a car" and keeps going through names, companies and gadgets of the period, including Banyan, dBase, Tandem, Lotus, adobe and Keuffel & Esser slide rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Each pair of lines says, "Back then this word meant something silly and ordinary." Like when a mouse was only an animal in the office.

sections.title: The Closing Toast
sections.content: The last lines turn to the future. "In accordance with Greenfield's Law", the poem toasts "exponential growth in memory and operating speed next year." The Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The poem ends by wishing for computers that get bigger and faster every year.
